passages.happening:
God tells Moses, “Command the Israelites to send away from the camp anyone with a skin disease, anyone who has a bodily discharge, and anyone who is defiled by a dead body” (verse 2).

The rule applies to ‘male and female alike’. The reason is given: ‘so they will not defile their camp, where I dwell among them’ (verse 3). The Israelites do as they are told (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
Chapters 1 to 4 gave the camp its shape. Chapters 5 and 6 turn to its condition. If God lives in the middle of Israel, then what happens anywhere in the camp matters to him.

The three conditions named here are the ones Leviticus 13 to 15 deals with at length: skin disease, bodily discharges, and contact with the dead. The Hebrew word for the skin disease, tsara'at, was once translated leprosy. It covered a range of conditions and was not limited to the illness now called by that name.

None of the three is a sin. This must be said plainly, because the passage is easy to misread. A person with a skin condition had done nothing wrong. Neither had someone who had buried a parent. These were states of the body linked with death and with the body's breaking down, and the tent of the living God was kept apart from the signs of death. Uncleanness in Leviticus is not guilt and it is not shame.

Being sent outside was painful. It was also, in most cases, for a time. Leviticus gave the way back: waiting, washing, and an offering. No one was sent out with no road home.

The Hebrew verb in verse 3, shakan, means to dwell or settle. From it comes the word for the tabernacle, mishkan, the dwelling. Later Jewish writers used a related word, Shekinah, for God's presence living among his people. These laws exist because God has chosen to live close by.
passages.later:
The three conditions of verse 2 read like a list of people Jesus met. A man with a skin disease knelt before him, and “Jesus reached out His hand and touched the man” (Mark 1:41). A woman who had bled for twelve years touched his cloak and was healed (Mark 5:25-29). He took a dead girl by the hand and raised her (Mark 5:41). Under the law, such contact made a person unclean. With Jesus the flow ran the other way, and they were made clean and whole.

Hebrews notes that Jesus himself died outside the city: ‘Jesus also suffered outside the city gate’ (Hebrews 13:12).
passages.hard:
Does this passage say that sick people are unclean, or that God wants them kept away?

No. It speaks of one camp at one time, with the tabernacle at its center, and of a ritual state, not of a person's worth or standing with God. It says nothing against any person who is ill today, and no one may use it to shut anyone out.

A word for anyone who has been made to feel unclean, by an illness, by your body or by your past. That is not what this book says of you. Your worth to God does not rise or fall with your body. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The people sent outside had done nothing wrong, and a way back was kept open for them. Ask who is on the outside of your community now because of illness, age or a death in the family. And ask what it would mean to go to them, as Jesus went to people the camp kept at a distance.

passages.t: Confess, repay, and add a fifth
passages.happening:
The next law concerns a wrong done to another person. “Tell the Israelites that when a man or woman acts unfaithfully against the LORD by committing any sin against another, that person is guilty and must confess the sin he has committed” (verses 6-7).

Confession is not the end of it. “He must make full restitution, add a fifth to its value, and give all this to the one he has wronged” (verse 7). If the wronged person has died and has no relative to receive it, the payment goes to the priest, together with a ram for atonement (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
The law moves inward, from the whole camp to the dealings of one neighbor with another.

Its first surprise is in verse 6. A wrong done to a neighbor is called acting ‘unfaithfully against the LORD’. The Hebrew verb, ma'al, means to break trust. To cheat a neighbor is to break faith with God, who lives in the same camp.

The law restates one in Leviticus (Leviticus 6:1-7) and adds to it. Confession is now required in so many words. It is not enough to feel sorry or to bring an offering quietly. The wrong must be named.

Then it must be put right. The offender pays back the whole amount and a fifth more. The extra fifth admits that a wrong costs the victim more than the thing taken. And the payment goes ‘to the one he has wronged’, not to the sanctuary. The priest receives it only when there is no one left to receive it.

That last case is new here. A person might be tempted to think that when the victim is dead and has no family, the debt has died too. The law says it has not. The debt is still owed, and it is owed to God.
passages.later:
The same order, the neighbor first and then the altar, is in the teaching of Jesus: “First go and be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift” (Matthew 5:24).

When Zacchaeus the tax collector met Jesus, he went beyond the fifth: ‘if I have cheated anyone, I will repay it fourfold’ (Luke 19:8).
passages.asks: The law asked for three things: say it, repay it, and add to it. Ask whether there is someone you have wronged to whom you have said sorry and given nothing back. And ask what full repayment, with something added, would look like in that case.

passages.t: When a husband suspects his wife
passages.happening:
The third law is about a husband who suspects his wife of adultery when there is no witness. Verse 14 names two cases side by side. The wife may have ‘defiled herself’. Or the jealousy may have come over him ‘even though she has not defiled herself’.

In either case, “he is to bring his wife to the priest”, with a plain offering of barley flour (verse 15). The priest has her stand before the LORD. He mixes holy water in a clay jar with dust from the tabernacle floor (verse 17). He loosens her hair and puts the offering in her hands (verse 18).

He puts her under oath. If she is innocent, the water will not harm her. If she is guilty, it will bring a curse on her body (verses 19-22). “Then the woman is to say, ‘Amen, Amen.’” The priest writes the curses on a scroll and washes the words off into the water, and she drinks it (verses 23-24).

The outcome is left to God. If she has been unfaithful, she will suffer (verse 27). “But if the woman has not defiled herself and is clean, she will be unaffected and able to conceive children” (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
This is one of the hardest passages in Numbers for a modern reader, and it should be read slowly and honestly.

Begin with the world it was given in. In ancient Israel a husband held legal authority over his wife. Suspicion of adultery was dangerous for her. Proven adultery carried death for both the man and the woman (Leviticus 20:10). But with no witness there could be no trial. A jealous husband and his relatives might then take matters into their own hands.

Other nations had tests for such cases. The Code of Hammurabi, from Babylon about 1750 BC, sent a wife accused by others to the river ordeal. She had to throw herself into the river, and the river god was held to judge her. An innocent woman could drown.

The rite in this chapter is different at each point. The case is taken out of the house and out of the husband's hands and brought before the priest and before God. The water holds only dust and washed-off ink, which could harm no one. No human court gives a verdict, and no human being carries out a sentence. If anything happens, it is God who does it. The law itself says the husband may be wrong: his jealousy may have come ‘even though she has not defiled herself’. And an innocent woman goes home cleared in public.

The details carry meaning. The loosened hair was a sign of mourning or shame. The barley offering has no oil or incense, like the sin offering of the poor (Leviticus 5:11). The curse is written and then washed into the cup, so that the woman takes the words into herself. What the curse on the body means is uncertain. The innocent woman is promised that she will be ‘able to conceive children’, which suggests that the curse touched the power to bear children.

The Mishnah, the collection of Jewish law compiled about AD 200, has a whole tractate on this rite, and records that it was given up in the first century.

None of this makes the passage easy. The hard question below faces what remains.
passages.later:
The prophets use the picture of an unfaithful wife for Israel's own unfaithfulness to God, and they turn it toward mercy. Through Hosea God says of his people, “Therefore, behold, I will allure her and lead her to the wilderness, and speak to her tenderly” (Hosea 2:14).

John's Gospel tells of a woman brought to Jesus by men who said she had been caught in adultery. They asked whether she should be stoned. He answered, “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to cast a stone at her” (John 8:7), and they went away one by one. The story is not in the oldest copies of John, as the note on John 8 explains, but the church has long treasured it.
passages.hard:
Is this law unfair to women? And does it give a husband the right to put his wife to a test?

The unfairness is real, and it should be admitted. There is no matching rite for a wife who suspects her husband. The woman is made to stand in public with her hair loosed because of a feeling her husband has. The law ends, ‘The husband will be free from guilt’ (verse 31), even if he was wrong. Some scholars read the rite chiefly as a tool of a husband's control. That reading sees something true.

Others, granting all this, point to what the rite held back. It took the case away from the husband. It used nothing that could injure. It left the verdict to God alone, so that no man could punish a wife on suspicion. Unlike the river ordeal, it could not kill an innocent woman. On this reading the law worked inside the order of its world and limited the harm that order could do. Jesus spoke this way about another law of Moses, the law of divorce: it was given ‘because of your hardness of heart’ (Matthew 19:8). A law can restrain a wrong without calling the world it restrains good.

Both things are true to the text, and these notes do not choose between them.

What the passage does not do is plain. It was a rite for Israel's tabernacle, carried out by a priest, and it ended long ago. It gives no husband today any right to test, watch, question or punish his wife. It is no warrant for suspicion or control of any woman. Jealousy that checks a partner's movements, messages or friendships is not godly care, and Scripture does not bless it.

Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are in an abusive marriage, seek safety first. Talk to a pastor or a counselor you trust, or call a local domestic violence line. These notes are not legal advice. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The law took a husband's suspicion out of his own hands and set it before God. Ask what suspicion or resentment you are holding against someone close to you, and whether you have treated your feeling as if it were proof. And ask how you speak of people who have been accused and never shown to be guilty.
